summary: Canada thistle is a thistle 1.5 to 5 feet tall with small light-purple (sometimes white) flower heads and pale green leaves with many spines along their edges. Unlike other thistles, it spreads through an extensive sideways root system, forming dense patches of connected plants, with male and female flower heads on separate plants. It grows mainly in open, wet to moist places such as pastures, wetlands, floodplains, roadsides and ditches. It pushes out native plants, lowering plant and animal diversity, and it also reduces farm crop yields and pasture productivity.
history: Despite its name, Canada thistle is native to Eurasia. It was brought to North America in shipments of agricultural seed, and it spreads by its roots and by people moving it around.

handling.text: Canada thistle spreads mostly through its roots, so mowing can hold it back but will not usually get rid of it. Infestations often need several control methods together and ongoing monitoring, and the whole patch needs treatment to stop it from resprouting. In New York City parks like Kissena, cutting, killing or removing plants without permission from NYC Parks is against park rules, so report it instead.

report:
New York's official database for invasive species sightings is iMapInvasives, run by the New York Natural Heritage Program (a partnership between SUNY ESF and the NYS Department of Environmental Conservation). You can make a free account and report directly to the online database, which is the preferred method, or use the iMapInvasives mobile app for iPhone and Android, which can upload your records once you have a connection again. If you don't want an account, the site has a public report form; those reports are reviewed by Natural Heritage Program staff each week before being added.

In New York City parks like Kissena Park, report what you find instead of removing it yourself. NYC Parks rules forbid cutting, killing or removing any plants, flowers, shrubs or other vegetation without permission from the Parks Commissioner, and forbid chasing, harassing, harming or removing any animal, nest, or the eggs of any amphibian, reptile or bird (56 RCNY §1-04).
